sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Deploying vision-language models (VLMs) on mobile devices is challenging due to their significant memory and compute requirements. We present a framework for quantizing VLMs for efficient inference on resource-constrained hardware. Our approach combines a quantization pipeline that uses the model itself to generate training data and does not require access to the training setup, with a novel 2.7-bit-per-parameter format supporting efficient execution on Arm CPUs. We validate our approach by compressing the Llama 3.2 11B Vision Instruct model to 3.7 GB with 8-bit activations, preserving strong performance on a set of standard visual question answering tasks.

sections.content: LLAMA-MOBILE: EFFICIENT 2.7-BIT QUANTIZATION OF VLMS Luka Ribar 1,, Jeevan Bhoot 2 and Douglas Orr 1 1Graphcore Research 2Arm Abstract Deploying vision-language models (VLMs) on mobile devices is challenging due to their significant memory and compute requirements. We present framework for quantizing VLMs for efficient inference on resource-constrained hardware. Our approach combines quantization pipeline that uses the model itself to generate training data and does not require access to the training setup, with novel 2.7-bit-per-parameter format supporting efficient execution on Arm CPUs. We validate our approach by compressing the Llama 3.2 11B Vision Instruct model to 3.7 GB with 8-bit activations, preserving strong performance on set of standard visual question answering tasks. Keywords vision-language models, quantization-aware training, model compression, numerical formats, mobile inference 1. Introduction Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated strong performance across difficult language tasks requiring complex reasoning and reading comprehension [24], [27], [29], [35]. Building on these capabilities, vision-language models (VLMs), such as Llama 3.2 Vision, Gemma 3, and Qwen3-VL [24], [30], [36], add vision encoder to the language model backbone, enabling the LLM to process and understand both image and text inputs. Such models are natural fit for mobile applications, but current systems often remain too computationally and memory-heavy for mobile deployment. Quantization is practical way to reduce model memory usage and improve inference efficiency with minimal performance degradation. However, aggressive low-bit quantization of VLMs remains In addition to selecting numerical format difficult in practice. that minimizes model degradation [15], [34], the quantization procedure itself is important [10], [23]. Quantization-aware training (QAT) is highly effective, but downstream performance is sensitive to training data selection [23], [28]. In this work, we address two practical constraints for VLM quantization: achieving sub-3-bit weight compression with efficient Arm CPU execution, and doing so without access to the original training data. First, we introduce S3D8, novel 2.7-bit-per-parameter quantization format that packs three signed weights into each byte through shared centroid index and decodes them to INT8 for inference. Second, because such aggressive compression can substantially degrade model quality, we use QAT procedure based on the models own generations. As previous similar approaches are not directly applicable to the multimodal setting [23], we introduce simple data-generation pipeline that preserves question-answering performance without directly fine-tuning on downstream tasks. We apply our framework to the Llama 3.2 11B Vision Instruct model [24] by compressing its weights to 3.7 GB while quantizing activations to 8-bit, showcasing limited degradation on set of standard visual-question answering tasks, as summarized in Figure 1. Our evaluation compares QAT with direct casting and GPTQ [10], strong PTQ baseline, to assess the effects of both the numerical format and the quantization procedure. Under our QAT scheme, our S3D8 format outperforms the standard INT with block-scaling, achieving approximately 22% extra compression for the same task performance. Directly casting model weights to fewer than 3.5 bits per parameter causes significant model degradation. While both GPTQ and QAT can improve performance, QAT is superior at fewer bits per parameter. We introduce novel 2.7-bit-per-parameter quantization format that enables efficient Arm CPU inference under aggressive model compression. We provide full VLM inference implementation for Arm CPUs on Linux and Android. We provide the full quantization pipeline and inference implementation at: graphcore-research/llama-mobile-vlm. 2. Related Work Quantization Quantized weights can be optimized either through post-training quantization (PTQ) techniques [10], [20] or QAT [23]. While PTQ offers less resource-intensive alternative, QAT is generally more effective, especially at low-bit widths, where quantization error tends to be significant [33]. The quantized values may be represented with uniform integer grids, floatingpoint values, or lookup tables, often accompanied with block, channel, or tensor-scaling, as well as vector quantization codes, including sign-factorized codebooks [14], [15], [19], [22], [37]. Recent VLM-oriented quantization work focused on effectively applying PTQ techniques in the multimodal setting [26], [32], [38]. Our work instead studies QAT for aggressive sub-3-bit VLM weight compression and treats the numerical format as part of the hardware co-design. Format co-design Hardware-aware format design and formataware kernel design are important avenues for practical formats. Gope et al. [31] explore weight layout, codebooks, and SIMD kernels for Arm CPUs, with practical implementation in llama.cpp Corresponding author: lukar@graphcore.ai 116 [16]. Our work employs similar techniques, but S3D8 uses vector format with potential for better ratedistortion trade-off than nonuniform scalar formats. In the extreme low-bit regime, Sherry [40] uses SIMD-friendly format for ternary quantization with structured sparsity at 1.25 bits per parameter. More broadly, hardware codesign has focused on block formats such as MXFP and NVFP4 [18], [42], which reduce the amount of computation in high precision. Similarly, DeepSeek V3 adapts their block scaling format to the available hardware by using large 2D blocks of weights to match GEMM hardware tile size [21]. Our work differs in that we co-design the numerical format around the SIMD decode path on Arm CPUs. 3. Method 3.1. Overview Our goal is to compress pretrained vision-language model into low-bit representation that can be effectively used for inference on low-resource Arm CPUs, while preserving the models visual question-answering ability. We focus on practical setting where we do not have access to the models original training data or recipe. This is particularly challenging problem, as aggressive quantization can lead to severe model degradation, especially in multimodal setting. To achieve an effective high level of compression, we use quantization-aware training with knowledge distillation, where the original full-precision model serves as teacher and the quantized model is trained to match its outputs. Since the effectiveness of QAT depends strongly on the training data distribution, we construct synthetic multimodal training set using the model itself. Once the target quantization format is specified, we apply consistent QAT procedure, enabling direct comparison between different numerical formats in our ablations. To enable efficient inference on Arm CPUs, we introduce 2.7-bit-per-parameter weight format that provides good balance between compression, model quality, and execution speed. The overall pipeline thus has the following components: 1. Synthetic Data Generation: Using the model itself, generate the training samples to be used for quantization-aware training. 2. Quantization-Aware Training: After choosing the numerical format of the quantized model, distill the original model using the synthetic data. 3. Mobile Deployment: Execute the model on Arm CPU, using the trained weights from the QAT stage. The remainder of this section first defines the common QAT objective used throughout the paper (Section 3.2), then describes the two components central to our approach: the synthetic datageneration pipeline (Section 3.3) and the proposed low-bit numerical format (Section 3.4). 3.2. Synthetic QAT Data Pipeline The main challenge in constructing data for multimodal quantization-aware training is that there is no direct analogue of the large-scale generic text corpora commonly used for languagemodel pretraining. While many multimodal datasets contain large numbers of image-caption pairs, such data is not necessarily well-matched to the behavior that an instruction-tuned VLM is expected to preserve. In particular, short descriptive captions provide only limited supervision for long-form generation, question answering, and instruction following, all of which are important for downstream VLM performance. Ideally, the QAT dataset should consist of images paired with diverse textual responses of varying length and style. The data should expose the model to range of different response types, including direct visual descriptions, short factual answers, as well as longer explanatory responses, while remaining sufficiently generic to avoid overfitting to particular task types. Although multimodal instruction datasets exist [13], [17], they may not match the original models response style or prompt format. We therefore use teacher generations as the text targets for distillation. For the image examples, we use ImageNet [4], which provides large and diverse collection of natural images, while remaining generic and independent of the downstream evaluation tasks. We then query the teacher model on these images, saving the models generated responses as the target sequences for knowledge distillation. Each final QAT sample consists of an image, sampled prompt, and the corresponding teacher-generated response sequence. Overall, our format at 2.68 bits per parameter leads to an average task degradation of 0.083, significantly outperforming other size-matched formats. The full performancecompression trade-off for these formats is shown in Figure 3a. Figure 1 compares direct casting, GPTQ, and QAT across range of model sizes. GPTQ improves over direct casting throughout most of the sweep, but QAT remains stronger at lower rates. At approximately 2.7 bits per parameter, S3D8 with GPTQ achieves an average task performance of 0.340, compared with 0.018 for rate-matched INT with GPTQ. Using the same quantization method for both isolates the effect of the weight format, showing that S3D8 retains substantially more accuracy than INT. Applying QAT to S3D8 further increases the average task performance to 0.661. Full GPTQ settings and implementation details are given in Section A.4. 4 4.2. Sampled vs. fixed prompts To measure the effect of prompt sampling (Section 3.3), we train fixed block-scaled INT3 format using either sampled prompts or single fixed prompt (``Describe the image:''), while varying the number of QAT steps (Figure 3b). Sampled prompting substantially improves downstream performance, suggesting that QAT benefits from diverse responses that probe range of instruction-following behavior. 4.3. Runtime Performance Our benchmarking analysis shows the practical efficiency of S3D8 as weight storage format on Arm CPUs. We test on the Android Pixel 8a in two modes: 5-core and 1-core, and on Graviton4 CPU consisting of 96 Arm Neoverse V2 cores. Full benchmarking configurations are given in Section D. First, we evaluate the speed of dequantization from S3D8 INT8. We perform multiple iterations with different S3D8 source tensors and shared destination tensor, to simulate the case where the dequantized tensor can remain in on-chip cache. We therefore report read bandwidth (not counting writes), and compare this against an INT8 copy with the same constraints an upper bound on achievable bandwidth. Results in Figures 8 and 9 show the low overhead of dequantization. For example, for the vision MLP up-projection on the Pixel 8a using 5 cores, S3D8 dequantization takes 133μs (16.5 GB/s), while the INT8 copy takes 310μs (21.2 GB/s). For larger 𝑚, the operation becomes compute-bound; since S3D8 dequantization implies extra work with arithmetic remaining INT8, we expect these results to match plain INT8 formats at best. The results in Table 2 support this, with speedup of S3D8 over INT8 for text generation, but slight slowdown for text prefill and vision encoding. 4.4. End-to-end Deployment on Arm CPUs We constructed custom C++ inference implementation of the Llama 3.2 11B Vision model. It includes custom file format based on safetensors [41] and efficient fused kernel implementations. We used this implementation to validate end-to-end support using S3D8 from model file of size 3.73 GB, including the vocabulary and metadata. To evaluate end-to-end performance, we generate 100 tokens from single image tile and short prompt and measure the token/s for the decoding phase, excluding model loading and image/text prefill. Our implementation achieves median 3.8 tokens/s (12.5 GB/s parameter read bandwidth) with S3D8 on the Pixel 8a an appreciable fraction of the maximum observed read bandwidth 25 GB/s. With parameters in INT8, the model does not fit in memory. On Graviton4, we obtain 36.8 tokens/s (120 GB/s) for S3D8 versus 26.4 tokens/s (258 GB/s) for INT8, showing practical speedup for singleuser text generation. 5. Limitations While our quantization framework is general, our experiments focus on single model, Llama 3.2 11B Vision Instruct, and on CPU execution. S3D8 uses an Arm-optimized 64-entry table lookup decoder; other architectures may require specialized kernels. Our evaluation also uses small set of VQA-style benchmarks that were part of the original Llama evaluation suite. We used fixed quantization format across all model weights; preliminary experiments with keeping selected layers in higher precision did not improve the accuracycompression trade-off. Finally, the prompt and image selection may be further optimized to improve downstream task generalization. 6. Conclusion We presented Llama-Mobile, framework for aggressively quantizing vision-language models for low-resource inference. Our approach combines synthetic multimodal data pipeline for quantization-aware distillation and S3D8, 2.7-bit-per-parameter weight format designed for efficient Arm CPU execution. Applied to Llama 3.2 11B Vision Instruct, the method compresses the model to 3.7 GB with 8-bit activations, while preserving good performance across set of VQA benchmarks. Our runtime performance analysis supports the practical efficiency of our method. Together, these results suggest that sub-3-bit VLM compression is viable route toward multimodal inference on resource-constrained devices. 6.1. Data Generation For the image database, we use the ImageNet [4] training set, which contains 1,281,167 images in total. To generate the image-text pairs for QAT, we sampled random prompt for each image and passed the image-prompt pair as inputs to the Llama 3.2 11B Vision Instruct model in bfloat16. The responses were sampled with temperature 0.6 and top_p = 0.9, with the maximum number of generated tokens set to 512, and each response was saved as text. The procedure leads to variable sequence length of the generated text, as the model can stop early once it generates the special <eot_id> token. This is desirable as it leads to the training data containing variable length responses based on the prompt, thus improving the diversity of the saved responses. For each sample, we generate the random prompt in the following way. In order to induce the instruction-tuned behavior, the Llama 3.2 11B Vision Instruct model uses the following template: <start_header_id>user<end_header_id>nn<image>{prompt}< eot_id><start_header_id>assistant<end_header_id>nn In order to keep the instruction-following behavior of the original model without breaking its ability to generate in the non-instruction setting, we apply the template with probability 𝑝temp = 0.75. With probability 1 𝑝temp we instead use the plain template: <image>{prompt} Next, we sample the prompt. First we sample the question part of the prompt, which is generic image-comprehension question that can be applied to most natural images. The question pool combines hand-written generic prompts, such as "Describe the image." or "Summarize the scene.", with generated prompts of the form {action} {target} {audience} {style}. For each generated prompt, we sample an action, such as "Describe" or "Explain", target, such as "the main subject" or "the key objects and their relationships", an audience, such as "for dataset annotation" or "for quick human review", and style, such as "using plain language" or "while explicitly noting uncertainty". This gives pool of 495 question prompts before instruction blocks are added. Once we generate the prompt, we prepend an additional instruction with probability 𝑝inst = 0.7. The instruction block always contains generic image-reasoning instruction, such as "Use simple language and avoid jargon". It may also contain an adherence probe, length probe, or format instruction, sampled independently with probabilities 𝑝adh = 0.4, 𝑝len = 0.75, and 𝑝fmt = 0.45, respectively. When length probe is used, short, medium, and long response constraints are selected with probabilities 0.40, 0.38, and 0.22, respectively. This biases the generated data toward concise responses while still including some longer visual explanations. Finally, for the fixed prompt experiments, we used the same "Describe the image:n" prompt for each image. Bit packing straightforward bit packing is [S2, S1, S0, Q4..0], where the lower 5 bits encode the centroid the S3D8 format for 10 Llama-Mobile: Efficient 2.7-Bit Quantization of VLMs supported in modern mobile CPUs. As the fastest format with wide availability at the time of this paper, it generally provides substantially higher arithmetic throughput than bfloat16 or float16. Vector Quantization The Arm SIMD instruction set includes TBL, which selects single bytes from lookup table of 16, 32, 48 or 64 elements. If using scalar quantization, common optimization is to form larger vector lookup tables rather than separately masking and shifting small indices. These vector lookup tables are the Cartesian product of the scalar centroids, so that in this case there is no runtime cost to replacing these with vector centroids. Absolute-Value Centroids & Sign Indicator Bits The most straightforward way to encode 3 values in an 8-bit vector format would be to encode single 8-bit centroid index into lookup table of shape (256, 3). However, this 768-byte lookup table is too large for SIMD registers. Since we expect the main benefit of VQ to come from shaping centroids to the distribution, not from particular covariance structures, we can exploit the symmetry expected and specify our 256 centroids as all 8 reflections of 32 absolute-value centroids. This allows for lookup table of shape (32, 3) with separate sign indicator bits (but note that we revise this lookup table layout with our next design decision). NSNQuant [37] uses related signfactorized construction for 8-dimensional KV-cache vector quantization, where separate sign bits accompany the codebook index. Fused sign lookups straightforward implementation of the format would look up the absolute value of each vector element, then unpack and apply the sign indicator bit for that element. We are not aware of fast way of doing this in Arm Advanced SIMD (simple approaches would use 4 instructions for each of the 3 elements to shift and apply twos complement). Our approach trades register pressure for instruction count by constructing lookup tables containing signed values, requiring 3 64-byte lookup tables in total. Bit layout We save 1 to 2 instructions by adopting the bit layout described in Section C.1, using permuted lookup tables. Since weight storage bit-packing and lookup table permutation can be performed once before loading the model, there is no runtime cost to doing this. Output channel packing While it might seem natural to pack elements of 𝑊 ℝ𝑛𝑘 that are consecutive on the reduction 𝑘-axis into single byte, this would require extra instructions to interleave weight elements, or unzip them from the input 𝑥 ℝ𝑘. Since kernel implementations that exploit instruction-level parallelism would typically compute multiple outputs in single pass through the inputs, it is straightforward to pack elements corresponding to consecutive output channels in each byte. This means that the only padding required is 3 𝑛/3 𝑛 on the output channels. D.
